Sample text:
---
There is a specific, quiet magic in opening a secondhand book and having something slip out from between the pages. 

Usually, it’s nothing monumental. It’s rarely a love letter or a treasure map. Most of the time, it is a piece of profoundly ordinary human ephemera: a faded receipt from a hardware store in Ohio dated October 2004; a torn corner of a lined notebook with *milk, batteries, call Sarah* scribbled in blue ink; a boarding pass for a flight from Chicago to Seattle, Seat 14A. 

Yet, holding that boarding pass feels like catching a ghost in the act of living. 

Suddenly, you aren’t just reading the story the author wrote; you are reading the shadow of the person who held this object before you. You look at the page where the ticket rested—say, page 182—and you have to wonder why they stopped there. Did the plane touch down in Seattle just as the protagonist made a terrible mistake, forcing the reader to snap the book shut, shove it into a carry-on, and step out into the rainy Pacific Northwest, never to pick the story back up again? Or did the person in Seat 14B strike up a conversation so captivating that the book was forgotten entirely?

We spend so much of our lives trying to curate how we are seen and how we will be remembered. We build monuments, write memoirs, and carefully edit our digital footprints. We smooth out our rough edges for the public eye. 

Because of that, there is something deeply comforting about these accidental time capsules. There is no pretension in a grocery list used as a bookmark. There is no performance in a hasty exclamation point penciled into the margin next to a passage about grief, or a coffee ring staining the corner of chapter four. These are the unguarded footprints of a mind simply passing through an afternoon. 

There is a word coined in the last decade—*sonder*—which describes the realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own. Used books are physical engines of sonder. They smell faintly of vanilla and dust (the charming chemical result of old paper breaking down), and they carry the literal weight of other people's quietest hours. Reading is mostly a solitary act, done in bedrooms, on crowded trains, in waiting rooms, and under trees. Yet, when you trace your finger over a sentence someone else underlined twenty years ago, the solitude breaks. For a split second, two strangers are sitting in the exact same room, looking at the exact same thing, nodding in agreement across a chasm of time.

I think about this whenever I finish a book I don't plan to keep. Before I drop it into a neighborhood Little Free Library or hand it over the counter at a used bookstore, I sometimes fight the urge to shake it out. Let the train ticket stay on page 94. Let the pressed, crumbling autumn leaf stay tucked in the epilogue. 

It’s nice to leave a note for the next traveler, even if all it says is: *I was here, I needed to buy batteries, and for a little while, I loved this story, too.*
---
